name: Avikam
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ahoua, Firmin. 2009. The Phonology-Syntax Interface in Avikam. Legon Journal of the Humanities 20: 123-149. DOI 10.4314/ljh.v20i0 (AJOL, open access:https://www.ajol.info/index.php/ljh/article/download/121554/111022). Kpanda dialect (Grand Lahou), fieldwork 1999.
catalog_quote: Avikam has two contrastive lexical tones, High and Low. It has also a downstepped High tone. There are no contrastive lexical Mid tones. The language has no contrastive contour tones on monosyllables, though it has, according to Hérault (1982:267), High-Low and Low-High contours on some syllables in initial, medial and final positions. In verbs, contour tones are clearly derived tones. A short glance at the lexicon (as for instance given in Hérault's (1982) Atlas, volume 2) provides minimal pairs of level tones. As mentioned above, CV words don't occur in isolation, so the contrastive pairs have all a prefix vowel. ... It should be noted that a High in a Low High sequence as in (1) is not automatically downstepped. The Downstep can be analysed as a floating tone that lowers following High tones but its position is not predictable, though it generally occurs word internally as in (2)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Avikam is a two-tone language (H, L, plus downstepped H) with lexical tonal minimal pairs; the article's prosodic constituents (tonal foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase) are defined by a Tone Lowering rule, and no word stress or accent is mentioned at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the tonal statement notes downstep position is unpredictable and surface contours (HL, LH) occur on some syllables per Hérault 1982:267.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (citation forms carry a prefix vowel; CV roots do not occur in isolation); the article is about tone across words and phrases in the Kpanda dialect of Grand Lahou.
new_statements.identity_note: Ahoua 2009 describes the Kpanda dialect of Avikam (Grand Lahou coast, fieldwork 1999); he notes at least two dialects differing only in minor segmental correspondences. Same language-level glottocode avik1243; no separate dialect glottocode found.

tone_statements.citation: Kossonou, Kouabena Théodore. 2020. De la non pertinence phonologique des tons modulés (descendants et montants) dans quelques langues kwa et gur de Côte d'Ivoire. Revue Africaine et Malgache de Recherche Scientifique (RAMReS) / CAMES: Littérature, Langues et Linguistique n°9 (1er semestre, juin 2020), 84-98.
tone_statements.quote: Dans les langues qui ont fait l’objet d’analyse, dans le cadre de cet article, on pourrait avancer que dans leur structure syllabique de type [CV], les consonnes sonores se trouvent (très souvent) systématiquement attestées dans des syllabes de tons phonétiquement réalisés modulés [HB] et [BH]. [...] (15) (a) dêgha (gur) (b) aïzi d’abra (kwa) (c) Ando (d) avikam [...] Les exemples sus mentionnés corroborent le fait que la réalisation des tons [HB] et [BH] est tributaire de la qualité de la consonne qui le précède : consonne sonore.
tone_statements.translation: In the languages analysed in this article, one may propose that in their [CV] syllable structure voiced consonants are (very often) systematically attested in syllables whose tones are phonetically realised as contours [HL] and [LH]. [...] (15) (a) Dêgha (Gur) (b) Aïzi of Abra (Kwa) (c) Ando (d) Avikam [...] The above examples corroborate the fact that the realisation of [HL] and [LH] tones depends on the quality of the preceding consonant: a voiced consonant.
tone_statements.locator: p. 93, section on consonant-tone interaction, example (15d) 'avikam'; abstract p. 84
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 level (H, B); contours [HB]/[BH] analysed as derived, non-phonemic

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 27 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: no hits). Sec. 4.2 p. 128: two contrastive lexical tones H and L plus downstepped H, no lexical Mid, no contrastive contours on monosyllables; the paper treats prosodic domains (tonal foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase) purely in terms of a Tone Lowering rule. Kpanda dialect, fieldwork 1999.

sources.note: Argues that rising/falling (modulated) tones in the languages examined, Avikam included, are not phonemic but surface sequences of H and B(L) on one vowel arising from vowel elision, tone spreading or a preceding voiced ('depressor') consonant; Avikam data (p. 93, ex. 15d: 'crabe', 'lever'..) illustrate [HB]/[BH] on CV syllables with voiced onsets. Consistent with Ahoua 2009 (H, L, no contrastive contours on monosyllables); Avikam tone letters were lost in text extraction.
